title: Don't quarrel
hook: don't dispute, or you'll lose heart and your strength will go (8:46)

segments.voice: Yesterday: between a man and his heart. Your line was he is nearer than my heart. Did you notice a turn in your mood? Today, what happens between people when hearts pull in different directions. Day four hundred nineteen.
screen: `BETWEEN A MAN AND HIS HEART — HE IS NEARER THAN MY HEART.`

segments.voice: A sailboat with two people at the helm, each pulling the tiller their own way, goes nowhere. The sail flaps. The boat turns in circles. Everyone's working hard, and all the work cancels out. Families do this. Teams do this. Whole communities do it, over things that look enormous at the time and tiny ten years later. Surah eight remembers a community that had just come through Badr, and would learn at Uhud what quarreling costs. Its verse forty-six uses the image of wind.
screen: `TWO PEOPLE AT THE TILLER.` → `THE SAIL FLAPS.` → `AN IMAGE OF WIND.`

segments.voice: In Pickthall's words: “dispute not one with another lest ye falter and your strength depart from you; but be steadfast!” The verse then adds: Allah is with the steadfast. The Arabic word for dispute is tanaza'u, from a root that means to pull, to snatch: two people tugging the same rope in opposite directions. It's not ordinary disagreement. Companions disagreed, about strategy, about meanings, about rulings, and the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ at times let the difference stand. Tanazu' is disagreement turned into a tug-of-war. And the result: fa-tafshalu, you'll lose heart, go slack, fail. And tadhhaba rihukum. Pickthall translates your strength will depart. Literally, your wind will go. In Arabic, a person's wind can mean their power, their momentum, the way we'd say the wind went out of their sails. Some early commentators also took it more literally: the wind of help that blows for a people at their best. Surah three, looking back on Uhud, describes what happened: a group lost heart, disputed over the order they'd been given, and disobeyed, and the day turned. The archers argued over whether to hold their post on the hill, and many left it. So surah eight isn't preaching from nowhere. It's naming a pattern the community would learn the hard way. And the answer it gives is not, never disagree. It's sabr: steadiness. Stay at your post. Hold your tongue when the argument has turned into tugging. Allah is with the steady ones.
screen: `TANAZU' — A TUG-OF-WAR.` · `DISAGREE, YES; PULL APART, NO.` · `YOUR WIND WILL GO.` · `THE ARCHERS AT UHUD.` · then, large: `QUARRELS WEAKEN.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe. Think of one quarrel you're carrying right now: a group chat argument, a sibling standoff, a cold war with a coworker, a debate you keep replaying in the shower. Ask honestly: is this still a disagreement, or has it become a tug-of-war? What would it cost you to let go of your end of the rope, just this one? Picture letting go. Notice the slack. The bell holds the time.
Don't quarrel. Surah eight, verse forty-six: don't pull against each other, or you'll lose heart and your wind will go; be steadfast. Today's word.
Your line: quarrels weaken. Today, drop one quarrel, or at least your end of it, and see what comes back into your sails. Day four hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Muslim teachers cite 8:46 when calling communities, families and mosque committees to unity, and distinguish respectful scholarly difference (ikhtilaf) from divisive quarreling (tanazu').

match.prompt: inside the verse — tap the pairs.

myth: companions disagreed often. it forbids tanazu', a tug-of-war that pulls a community apart.
the Arabic for your strength will depart says, literally, your wind will go
tadhhaba rihukum: like the wind going out of your sails.
surah three links the setback at Uhud to disputing over orders
the archers argued over holding their post, and many left it.

fork.setup: you're one of the archers on the hill at Uhud. it looks like the battle is won, and your group starts arguing whether to stay. what did the order say?
fork.reveal: they were told to hold their post. many left it after disputing, and the day turned (3:152).

original.note: Arabic: and do not dispute, do not pull against one another (8:46).

trapdoor: what it means: disagree if you must, but don't turn it into a tug-of-war; it drains a people's heart and strength.
what a scholar hears: rih in 8:46 is glossed by exegetes as power and momentum, by some as the wind of divine help; scholars separate permitted ikhtilaf from blameworthy tanazu'.

sources.quoted: dispute not one with another lest ye falter and your strength depart from you; but be steadfast!

notes: Bukhari 3039 (the archers at Uhud) cited from memory; confirm.
Uhud dated a year after Badr (3 AH); confirm.
Readings of rih (power/momentum vs. wind of help) summarized; confirm.
Root n-z-' glossed as to pull/snatch; confirm.
